en: Now we have this rough plan or these steps
here that help us solve problems.
Now an important part of solving problems
and coming up with algorithms
often is that you simplify problems.
And you got a couple of tools there as well,
a couple of things that you can look into
when you're facing a problem and you're not
sure how you wanna tackle it.
One very common approach of simplifying a
problem is to split it into smaller
subproblems.
That's something we did a couple of times in
this course that can involve that you split
arrays into smaller chunks.
We did, for example, do that in some sorting
algorithms.
That can also involve,
possibly combined with splitting arrays into
chunks, that you use recursion. You saw that
in various parts of this course as well, for
example, in the permutations algorithms.
So recursion and/or splitting arrays into
chunks, that sometimes is something that can
help you. Now you won't be able to do this
on every algorithm. Some problems just can't
be solved with
recursion, or recursion won't really help
you at least. And some problems also don't
use arrays at all, so there's nothing you
could split into chunks. But quite a lot of
algorithms actually will embrace
one of these techniques, and therefore
that's definitely something you might wanna
consider.
Now another very obvious obvious
thing that can help you with simplifying a
problem is that you
add a couple of console.log statements or
you use breakpoints to verify
your solution, your temporary variables,
your intermediate results.
And there's nothing wrong with doing that in
an interview situation, by the way. If you
explain why you're doing that, if you
explain what you're checking right now, for
example, that you're now checking whether
you did reformat the input correctly, That's
absolutely fine. It's way better to early
check your intermediate results than to
write down an entire algorithm 10 minutes or
15 minutes long
just to then see that it's totally wrong and
that some early step is totally wrong. So
definitely check your intermediate results
and look into your code,
especially with recursion. It sometimes can
be hard to predict
which value will be in which function
execution. And a couple of console.log
statements, as we also did it in this
course, can really help you with that.
Now last but not least, another very helpful
thing to do
is that you use helper variables, for
example helper arrays, helper objects to
store intermediate results.
Sometimes you can solve problems with inline
solutions. So for example, by editing the
original input array you're getting or
anything like that. And often you can also
shorten code instead of writing for loops
and so on. Sometimes you can shorten code,
but
that can also make it harder to understand
the solution. That can also make it harder
to come up with a solution.
So don't worry too much about space
complexity or
long code. Instead, really write code that
you understand. Make it clear what you're
storing where
And well, simply make your code as easy to
understand as possible because in the end,
not just your interview partner or your
colleagues need to understand the code, you
also need to do that and you should also
understand it if you come back in a day or
two.
So these are some
things, some thoughts on how you might wanna
simplify problems
that can apply to algorithms, especially the
second and the third step apply to pretty
much all algorithms.
And therefore, you should use these tools to
have an easier time coming up with
algorithms and solving problems.
